m: Om. I worship in the heart Kameshvari, lovely as heated gold, whose eyes are the sun, the moon, and fire, who holds with her beautiful arms the bow, arrows, goad, noose, and spear, whose form is the power of Shiva, and who wears the crescent moon.
Om. The seer said:
Seeing his brother Nishumbha slain, a brother equal to his own life, and seeing his army being destroyed, Shumbha spoke in anger.
Durga, you who are spoiled by the arrogance of strength, do not be proud. Relying on the strength of others, you fight, exceedingly conceited.
The Goddess said:
I alone am here in the world. What second other than me is there? Look, wicked one: these powers of mine are entering into me alone.
Then all those goddesses, Brahmani foremost among them, went to rest in the body of that Goddess. Ambika then stood alone.
The Goddess said:
When I stood here in many forms by my many powers, that has been drawn back. I stand alone. Be steady in the fight.
The seer said:
Then a dreadful battle began between the Goddess and Shumbha, the two of them, as all the gods and the asuras looked on.
With showers of arrows, with sharp weapons, and with very dreadful missiles, their battle again became a terror to all the worlds.
Whatever divine missiles Ambika released by the hundred, the lord of the daityas broke them with counter-weapons.
The supreme sovereign, with a mere play of fierce humkaras and the like, broke the divine missiles he had released.
Then that asura covered the Goddess with hundreds of arrows. The Goddess, angered, cut his bow with her own arrows.
When the bow was cut, the lord of the daityas took up a spear. The Goddess cut that too with her discus, even as it remained in his hand.
Then the lord of the daityas, taking a sword and a shield bright with a hundred moons, shining like the sun, rushed at the Goddess.

As he came on, Chandika quickly cut the sword with sharp arrows shot from her bow, and the shield that was bright as the sun's rays. She also brought down the horses, and the chariot together with the charioteer.
His horses slain, his bow cut, his charioteer gone, the daitya then seized a terrible hammer, intent on Ambika's death.
She cut the hammer of the one who was rushing in, with sharpened arrows. Even so, he rushed at her with force, his fist raised.
That bull among daityas brought his fist down on the Goddess's heart. The Goddess struck him in the chest with her palm.
Struck by the blow of her palm, the king of the daityas suddenly fell to the ground, and then rose again in the same way.
Leaping up, he seized the Goddess and rose high into the sky. There too, with no support, Chandika fought him.
The daitya and Chandika then wrestled with each other in the sky, a fight that first caused wonder to the siddhas and the sages.
After wrestling with him for a long time, Ambika lifted him, whirled him about, and threw him onto the ground.
Thrown down, he reached the earth and, evil-minded, rushed forward with force, fist raised, wishing to slay Chandika.
As he came, the Goddess, with her spear, pierced the chest of that lord of all the daitya people and threw him onto the earth.
His life gone, pierced by the tip of the Goddess's spear, he fell upon the ground, shaking the whole earth with its oceans, islands, and mountains.
When that evil-minded one was slain, the whole world became glad. The world obtained great ease, and the sky became clear.
The portent-clouds that had come before, with their meteors, grew calm. The rivers kept to their courses when he had been felled.
Then all the hosts of gods became filled with joy when he was slain, and the gandharvas sang beautifully.
Others played instruments, and the bands of apsarases danced. Auspicious winds blew, and the sun became brightly radiant.
The fires blazed peacefully, and the sounds born of the directions grew quiet.
